Turn three notes into useful chord shapes.

Written by Jean-François Seignemorte · Reviewed 27 October 2026

What is a triad?

A triad is a three-note chord built from a root, a third and a fifth. A major triad uses a major third; a minor triad uses a minor third. Inversions keep the same notes but change which one is lowest.

What is a triad?
ChordNotesFormula
A majorA · C♯ · E1 · 3 · 5
A minorA · C · E1 · ♭3 · 5

Begin on the three highest strings

An A minor shape on strings G–B–E at fret 5 gives C–E–A, from lower to higher string. It is a first inversion because C, the third, is the lowest note in this voicing. Play each note separately before strumming all three.

  1. Open Learn and choose Triads. Keep the root A and select minor.
  2. Choose a group of three strings and inspect the available inversions. Find the root in each shape.
  3. Move to another inversion, name its notes and listen to how the voicing changes while the chord stays A minor.

Practice the small change between major and minor

Compare A major and A minor. A and E remain the same; C♯ moves down one semitone to C. Use the degree labels to locate the third and hear that change.

The Daily Routine includes a guided triad exercise. Microphone feedback is a practice aid and can depend on how clearly the notes are played and captured. Manual practice remains available.

Questions before you start

Are triads the same as full barre chords?

A triad contains three chord tones. A larger guitar chord can repeat those tones across more strings. Triad practice helps you see the smaller voicings inside larger shapes.

Can I change inversions and string groups?

Yes. The guitar Learn view includes triad string-group controls and shows root position and inversions.
